No cash cost. Unstable schedules are a leading reason hourly staff quit; the capacity and quality penalties are game-balance values standing in for no-shows and quits.
2.5 hires a year (50% turnover of five) x 30 paid hours x $18 = $1,350 a year = $113 a month.
$113 plus a monthly two-hour paid tasting for five people (10 h x $21 = $210) = $323, rounded to $330. A roaster's lab day is assumed free with a wholesale account.
Staff lose about $1.57 an hour of card tips ($3.13 to $1.56, extra.tips); modelled as a 3% capacity loss through quits. Reputation +0.01 for customers tired of tip screens. Game-balance values.
$3 x 640 barista hours = $1,920, plus 11.58% employer payroll taxes = $2,142. Tips of $3.13 an hour are replaced by a certain wage.
No cash cost; the violation arises because New York limits required tip pools to customer-service staff and bars managers outright.
4 full-timers x $250 = $1,000. A QSEHRA may reimburse up to $6,450 a year ($537.50 a month) for one person in 2026 and needs no group plan; available to employers with fewer than 50 full-time staff.
8 hours a week of shifts kept for a trained extra part-timer x $19 x 4.33 = $658.
60 h a week = 260 h a month, 100 h more than the 160 the pack assumes: 100 / 1,280 team and owner-equivalent hours = +8% capacity. Fatigue is handled in extra.mechanics.owner_hours_and_burnout.
Demand -2% stands in for 2% of sales lost to skimming and free drinks; vendor figures put employee theft near 4% of restaurant sales, which I halve for a small owner-present shop.
My estimate of a team-management add-on to the register, $35 to $60 a month. Not a quote.
$60 plus about $100 for cloud camera storage and the paid half-hour weekly count. My estimate.
5 people x 1 paid hour x $21 / 12 = $8.75, rounded to $10.
2.5 hires a year x $300 of sponsored posts / 12 = $62.
2.5 hires a year x 4 finalists x 3 h x $17 / 12 = $42.50, rounded to $50.
$1,824 a year / 12 = $152 (one broker's small-business average); small restaurants are quoted $800 to $3,000 a year. Wage-and-hour claims are usually excluded.

taxCredits.name: Credit for employer Social Security and Medicare taxes paid on tips
taxCredits.base: reported tips above what is needed to reach $5.15 an hour
taxCredits.note: Arithmetic: 7.65% x $2,000 of reported card tips = $153 a month, $1,836 a year, which cancels the pack's monthly cost "Employer payroll tax on reported tips". It is a credit against the owner's income tax, so it helps only a profitable shop, and the same tax cannot also be deducted. The $5.15 floor is from memory of Internal Revenue Code section 45B; search-seen (primary, irs.gov): the credit is claimed on Form 8846.

laborBenchmarks.note: Search-seen (secondary, vendor guides): coffee shops run labor at 30% to 35% of sales; the National Restaurant Association median for limited service is $45.33 of sales per labor hour (quoted by a vendor). Arithmetic for the pack's reference month: $51,000 / 640 paid staff hours = $79.69; wages plus employer taxes ($13,440 + $1,556) / $51,000 = 29.4% before the owner's own hours, which the pack values at $4,800 more. The existing benchmark of 35% therefore holds only if the owner's work is counted.

peopleCalendar.what: Slowest sales of the year: cut hours and part-timers leave, keep hours and labor runs over 40% of sales. W-2 forms are due by January 31 and now carry a tipped-occupation code. The 32 unpaid protected hours reset for everyone on January 1.
Flu and stomach bugs: expect several sick calls in the same fortnight. No doctor's note may be asked for three days or less.
Spring hiring starts. Post jobs before the patios open and the summer squeeze begins.
First-quarter payroll returns (Form 941, NYS-45) are due April 30. Check that tips ran through payroll all quarter.
Finals and graduation: student baristas cut hours, then leave. The summer hiring squeeze begins.
School is out: workers of 16 and 17 may work longer days, up to 48 hours a week. Heat behind the bar.
Vacation requests peak. Second-quarter payroll returns are due July 31.
Thinnest roster of the year: vacations and departures before the fall term.
Students are back and looking for shifts: the easiest hiring month. Workers under 18 return to school-night limits (4 hours, done by 10 pm).
Third-quarter payroll returns due October 31. Holiday time-off requests arrive. Health plan open enrollment begins. The state publishes next year's minimum wage by October 1.
Thanksgiving week: everyone wants the same days. Decide the holiday schedule in writing early.
Holiday rush with a short roster: overtime and long days. Yearly harassment prevention training must be done for anyone hired a year ago. Workers' compensation policy audit follows the policy year.

extra.peopleCalendarNote: A planning calendar built from the rules and patterns in this fragment; due dates for Forms 941 and NYS-45 (the last day of the month after each quarter) and W-2 (January 31) are from memory, not opened this session.

eventCatalog.name: The opener does not show up
eventCatalog.text: It is 6:40 am, the door is locked and the opener is not answering the phone. The morning rush starts in 20 minutes.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Scheduling set to "night before", or pay under the market wage, for two months in a row.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Food preparation and serving workers had a 4.0% absence rate in 2025, against 3.2% for all workers (BLS, quoted by Deputy).
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: one lost morning is about a third of one day's sales, 1 / 90 of the month; three in a month is 3%. My estimate of three.

eventCatalog.name: A trained barista gives two weeks' notice
eventCatalog.text: One of your experienced baristas found a job closer to home. Two weeks from now you are one person short.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A worker's tenure pressure reaches 1 (extra.mechanics.turnover_and_replacement): market pay, no benefits, about 24 months on the job.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Monthly quits in accommodation and food services ran 3.6% to 5.0% in June to September 2026 (BLS JOLTS); median tenure in food preparation and serving was 2.2 years in January 2026 (BLS).
eventCatalog.note: Cash: hard replacement cost per hourly worker, Black Box Intelligence 2025. Capacity: one of five people replaced by a trainee at 40% to 85% speed for three months averages about 8% lost.

eventCatalog.name: Quit by text, mid-week
eventCatalog.text: "Not coming back, sorry." No notice, and tomorrow's close has nobody on it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Scheduling set to "night before", a wage shortcut in force, or tips cut, for three months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not measured separately; 70% of workers aged 16 to 19 have been with their employer 12 months or less (BLS tenure, January 2024).
eventCatalog.note: One of five people gone with no overlap = 20% for a month. A temp barista from a staffing app costs $29 to $40 an hour in New York City (the platform's own rate page).

eventCatalog.name: Your shift lead gets an offer from a chain
eventCatalog.text: A chain offers your lead a supervisor job with benefits. The lead tells you before answering.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Lead pay within $1 of chain postings, no benefits, for six months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2026 postings: a venture-backed chain lists shift leads at $21 an hour; the largest chain's flagship pays baristas $19.31 after certification.
eventCatalog.note: With the pack's $24 lead wage this does not fire by default. The lead usually holds a Food Protection Certificate, so see certificate_holder_leaves.

eventCatalog.name: The only other certificate holder quits
eventCatalog.text: The person who left was the one who ran the shop with a Food Protection Certificate on your days off.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Fewer than three certificate holders (owner included) and one of them leaves.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from turnover: with two holders and 50% yearly turnover, a gap is expected within the year.
eventCatalog.note: Until a new holder passes the exam (14 days in the pack) the owner must be on site every open hour, or shifts run uncovered: $400 and 10 points per inspection (existing violation no_food_protection_cert).

eventCatalog.name: New hire works three shifts and disappears
eventCatalog.text: You paid for 15 hours of training. On day four the new barista stops answering.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Hiring by word of mouth with no paid trial and no references.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Short tenure is the norm for the youngest workers: 70% of those aged 16 to 19 have 12 months or less with their employer (BLS).
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: 15 h x $18 + employer taxes = about $300. The vacancy restarts.

eventCatalog.name: Trainee alone on bar at 8:30 am
eventCatalog.text: The line is out the door and the newest hire is pulling shots. Drinks come out slow and wrong.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Training set to "shadow only" while a hire is in the first six weeks.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Operators put new baristas on register and bar-back for two to six weeks before the bar (Perfect Daily Grind).
eventCatalog.note: Effects are my estimates from the skill ramp in extra.staffModel.

eventCatalog.name: Two people out, two people at 55 hours
eventCatalog.text: You never replaced the baristas who left. The ones who stayed are covering, and the payroll report shows 30 overtime hours a week.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Paid hours needed by the schedule exceed 40 a week per person for a full month.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from the roster. Overtime is 1.5 times the regular rate after 40 hours in a week (12 NYCRR 146-1.4).
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: 30 overtime hours a week x 4.33 x $10.50 premium = $1,364 on a $13,440 payroll = +10%. Fatigue then raises the tenure pressure of the people covering.

eventCatalog.name: Open-to-close doubles
eventCatalog.text: Someone works 6:30 am to 7:30 pm with a long break in the middle. The day spans 13 hours.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Any scheduled day whose first clock-in and last clock-out are more than 10 hours apart.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from the schedule: one extra hour at the $17.00 minimum for each such day, whatever the worker's wage (12 NYCRR 146-1.6).
eventCatalog.note: The amount is per day and per worker; ten doubles a month cost $170.

eventCatalog.name: The drawer is short again
eventCatalog.text: Third time this month the cash count is $60 to $180 under the register report.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Cash controls set to "trust" for two months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Vendor figures put employee theft near 4% of restaurant sales and 75% of inventory shrink (attributed to the National Restaurant Association, second-hand). A Washington coffee-stand barista skimmed about $1,600 and staged a robbery to hide it.
eventCatalog.note: The 2% is my estimate for a small owner-present shop. Taking the shortage out of pay is illegal (violation illegal_deductions).

eventCatalog.name: The deposits never reached the bank
eventCatalog.text: Your accountant finds that several cash deposits recorded by the manager were never made.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A hired manager handles deposits and cash controls stay on "trust" for six months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reported cases: a South Carolina cafe manager, over $12,000, found by the accountant's audit; an Iowa coffee-store manager, about $18,400 in five months of 2025; a chain store manager, $37,896 in 25 missing deposits.
eventCatalog.note: Game value is the smallest of the three reported cases.

eventCatalog.name: Free drinks for friends
eventCatalog.text: Milk and beans are running out faster than the register says they should.
eventCatalog.realSignal: One shared register login and no void or discount report for three months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No clean statistic; void and refund schemes show a median loss of about $1,200 a month in fraud studies quoted by a vendor.
eventCatalog.note: The 2% on cost of goods is my estimate (about $265 a month at the reference point). A written shift-drink allowance removes most of it.

eventCatalog.name: Morning crew against closing crew
eventCatalog.text: The openers do most of the sales; the closers do the cleaning and get the smaller jar. Two people stop speaking.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Tip rule set to "each shift keeps its own" or no written rule, for two months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Tip disputes were part of the 2023 Nashville and 2026 California coffee-shop walkouts.
eventCatalog.note: A pool split by hours worked with a posted sheet is the common fix; records of the pool must be kept six years (12 NYCRR 146-2.17).

eventCatalog.name: A former barista files a wage claim
eventCatalog.text: A letter from the state Labor Department asks for six years of schedules, time records, pay stubs and pay notices for the whole staff.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Any wage shortcut in force during the employment of a worker who then leaves.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: In 2025 the state Labor Department recovered more than $35 million in stolen wages from more than 5,000 employers, the most since 2015.
eventCatalog.note: The audit covers every worker, not only the one who complained. The lawful move is to stop the shortcut and pay what is owed before the investigator computes it; an employment practices policy does not cover wage claims.

eventCatalog.name: A barista asks why the overtime is missing
eventCatalog.text: One of your team has done the arithmetic on the pay stub and asks, politely, in front of the others.
eventCatalog.realSignal: An overtime, call-in or spread-of-hours shortcut in force for one month.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Most labor cases begin with one worker's question or complaint (state Labor Department process).
eventCatalog.note: Paying the difference now costs 1.0 x; a claim later costs 2.0 x; punishing the worker adds the retaliation penalty.

eventCatalog.name: Notice of potential charges
eventCatalog.text: The state tells you that someone you let go has claimed unemployment benefits and that your account may be charged.
eventCatalog.realSignal: You fire or lay off a worker, or cut their hours to 30 a week or fewer.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The maximum weekly benefit rose from $504 to $869 on October 13, 2025; 2026 employer rates run 1.7% to 9.5%, new employers 4.1%.
eventCatalog.note: Search-seen (primary, NY DOL employer guide IA 318.2): the last employer is charged seven times the weekly benefit first, the rest is shared by wage history, up to 26 weeks; no charge for misconduct or a quit without good cause if the employer answers on time. Arithmetic: a $21, 40-hour barista earns $10,920 a quarter; benefit about 1/26 of that = $420; 7 x $420 = $2,940 charged. The 1/26 rule is from memory.

eventCatalog.name: A regular will not leave a barista alone
eventCatalog.text: He comes every day, comments on her body and waits for her shift to end. She tells you she is scared.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Announced for every shop on the block at the same time; what follows depends on the complaint-handling choice.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No count found. New York's Human Rights Law makes the employer liable for harassment by customers once it knows and fails to act.
eventCatalog.note: Banning the customer costs one regular (about 0.2% of sales, my estimate). Ignoring it leads to the violation harassment_complaint_ignored and usually to a resignation.

eventCatalog.name: Two baristas complain about the shift lead
eventCatalog.text: They say the lead makes jokes about their accents and gives the bad shifts to whoever objects.
eventCatalog.realSignal: No harassment policy or training for six months, or a lead given power over schedules.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Employment claims cost small businesses $27,000 to $54,000 a case on average (an insurer's figure).
eventCatalog.note: Discrimination by national origin is covered the same way as sexual harassment; the state law applies to every employer.

eventCatalog.name: The staff hand you a petition
eventCatalog.text: All four baristas have signed a letter asking for steadier schedules and a raise. One mentions a union.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Hours cut and pay at or under market and a complaint ignored, within three months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A Brooklyn coffee shop's staff filed for a union unanimously in November 2022 after hours and pay were cut; small chains in the city followed in 2023 and 2024.
eventCatalog.note: The 7% is a $1.50 raise on $21. Acting together about pay is protected with or without a union, in a shop of any size.

eventCatalog.name: The whole team walks out
eventCatalog.text: A sign on the door reads "closed for staff issues". Nobody came in today.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A late or missed payroll, or tips withheld, for two pay periods.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reported cases: a California coffee house closed after a walkout over unpaid wages and tips (March 2026); in Kansas City nine of ten staff quit together (2023); Nashville locations closed after a walkout over tips (2023).
eventCatalog.note: Five closure days is my estimate of the time to pay up and rehire enough people to open.

eventCatalog.name: Payroll Friday and the account is short
eventCatalog.text: Rent cleared on Monday. Friday's payroll is $3,100 and the balance is $1,900.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Cash on hand below one week of payroll on payday.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: In a survey of 391 restaurant owners, 51% had gone without their own paycheck in the past year to make payroll (Clarify Capital, quoted in trade press).
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: $13,440 / 4.33 = $3,104 a week. Wages come first: paying staff late is the fastest route to a walkout and to the pay-frequency violation.

eventCatalog.name: A barista is burned at the steam wand
eventCatalog.text: Rushing through the line, a barista scalds a hand, or slips on a wet floor behind the bar, and needs urgent care.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Cleaning set to "wipe and go" or the roster stretched thin for three months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: In an insurer's study of restaurant claims (2013 to 2017) cuts were about a third of claims and slips and falls paid 4.5 times as much; cafes lost 45% more work time than other restaurants.
eventCatalog.note: With a policy the insurer pays treatment and lost wages. Without one you pay both, and the state adds up to $2,000 for every 10 days uninsured (_common violation no_wc_insurance).

eventCatalog.name: Your fastest barista develops wrist pain
eventCatalog.text: Tamping and steaming 300 drinks a day has caught up with your best barista. The doctor says rest.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The same person on the espresso machine for nearly every rush for 12 months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: "Barista wrist" claims took an average of 366 days to return to work in the same insurer's study.
eventCatalog.note: Rotating stations and training a second strong bar person are the lawful moves; the capacity loss is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Workers' compensation audit
eventCatalog.text: The insurer audits last year's payroll. You grew, and you paid a cleaner in cash who had no insurance of their own.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Actual payroll above the estimate given to the insurer, or payments to uninsured contractors, at the policy anniversary.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every policy is audited after its year; payments to uninsured subcontractors are added to payroll.
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: $40,000 of extra payroll x the 2% planning rate in _common = $800. The 2026 state loss cost for the restaurant class (9072) is $1.03 per $100 of payroll before the insurer's multiplier (Workers' Compensation Board class list).

eventCatalog.name: You have not had a day off in eleven weeks
eventCatalog.text: You forget an order to the dairy, snap at a regular and fall asleep doing the books.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Own hours at 80 a week for three months, or 60 for nine.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 78% of hospitality business owners reported burnout in a 2024 survey (Bionic, quoted second-hand); restaurant general managers average 55 to 60 hours a week.
eventCatalog.note: Effects are game-balance values. An LLC owner has no paid sick leave, no unemployment insurance and no workers' compensation unless bought.

eventCatalog.name: You are sick and nobody else can open
eventCatalog.text: You have the only keys, the only alarm code and the only Food Protection Certificate.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The owner is the only certificate holder or key holder.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from the setup; the 4.0% absence rate applies to owners too.
eventCatalog.note: Two days is my estimate. Certifying two leads costs about $770 once (setup item extra_food_protection_certs).

eventCatalog.name: The manager you rely on resigns
eventCatalog.text: After six months of 50-hour weeks at the lowest legal salary, your manager takes a job with a restaurant group.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Manager paid at the exempt floor and working over 45 hours a week for six months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Food service managers in the New York metro averaged $93,730 a year in May 2025 (BLS), 41% above the $66,300 exempt floor.
eventCatalog.note: The owner goes back to 60 to 80 hours until a replacement is found.

eventCatalog.name: Your fifth employee makes sick leave paid
eventCatalog.text: With five people on payroll, every worker's 40 hours of safe and sick leave must now be paid.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Headcount reaches five employees, part-timers included.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from headcount.
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: 5 x 40 h x $21 / 12 = $350 a month if every hour is used (the pack's line "Paid sick leave cover", $70 per worker). With four employees the same hours are protected but unpaid.

eventCatalog.name: Ten employees: the state retirement program applies
eventCatalog.text: A letter says you must register for New York Secure Choice or certify that you offer a retirement plan.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Ten or more employees for a full calendar year and two years in business.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2026 registration deadlines: March 18 (30 or more employees), May 15 (15 to 29), July 15 (10 to 14).
eventCatalog.note: No employer contribution; the work is payroll set-up. Penalties had not been announced when the sources were written. A one-shop cafe rarely reaches ten.

eventCatalog.name: A new hire takes protected time in week one
eventCatalog.text: On the third shift your new barista calls in: a child is sick. The 32 unpaid protected hours are available from the first day.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Any hire after February 22, 2026.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: New rule: Local Law 145 gives every worker 32 unpaid hours on hire and again each January 1.
eventCatalog.note: You may not ask for a note for three days or less, nor make the worker find a replacement ($500 per instance).

eventCatalog.name: Regulars ask where your barista went
eventCatalog.text: The barista who knew sixty orders by heart has left. A few regulars now stop at the place where she works.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A barista with 12 months or more at the shop leaves.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No measurement found; owners describe it often.
eventCatalog.note: The 2% for two months is my estimate and should be treated as a design value.

eventCatalog.name: One-star review: "the barista rolled her eyes"
eventCatalog.text: A new review describes a slow line and a short-tempered barista on her eleventh straight day.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Roster stretched (no day of rest, overtime creep) or training on "shadow only" for two months.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: See the demand researcher's part for how ratings move sales.
eventCatalog.note: Effect size is a game-balance value.

eventCatalog.name: A former barista posts about the tips
eventCatalog.text: A video about "where the tip jar really goes" at your shop is passed around the neighborhood.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shortcut keep_tips or manager_in_tip_pool in force when a worker leaves.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Tips were a stated cause of the 2023 Nashville walkout and the 2026 California one, both covered by local news.
eventCatalog.note: Effects are game-balance values; the legal bill is the tip_theft or tip_pool_ineligible violation.

eventCatalog.name: School starts: your 17-year-old cannot close
eventCatalog.text: From September the student who closed all summer may work 4 hours on school nights and must be done by 10 pm.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A worker under 18 on the roster when school starts.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from the roster and the school calendar.
eventCatalog.note: Working papers move to a state database on May 9, 2027; fines for a first violation now reach $10,000.

eventCatalog.name: January: sales drop, hours get cut
eventCatalog.text: Fewer customers until March. Either you cut shifts, and part-timers start looking, or you keep them and labor eats the month.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The slowest sales months of the year (see the demand researcher's monthly index).
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly pattern.
eventCatalog.note: Cutting a shift after the worker has arrived costs call-in pay (3 hours). Hours cut to 30 a week or fewer also require the unemployment notice (Record of Employment).

eventCatalog.name: Finals and summer break
eventCatalog.text: College terms end. Student baristas cut their hours for exams, then leave the city for the summer.
eventCatalog.realSignal: University term dates: finals in May, summer break from late May.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly pattern near every campus.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events; the 7% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: September: students are back and looking for shifts
eventCatalog.text: The fall term starts. Applications double, and people with barista experience are among them.
eventCatalog.realSignal: University term dates: the fall term begins in late August or early September.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly pattern.
eventCatalog.note: The best month to rebuild the bench before the holidays; the 3% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Holiday week: everyone wants the same days off
eventCatalog.text: Thanksgiving through New Year. Half the team asks for the same days.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The calendar.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly pattern.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events. A holiday schedule fixed in October is the cheap move; New York law requires no holiday premium pay.

eventCatalog.name: Summer hiring squeeze
eventCatalog.text: Every patio, rooftop and ice cream window is hiring at once.
eventCatalog.realSignal: National Restaurant Association summer hiring forecast; job-board posting counts.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About 450,000 seasonal restaurant jobs were projected for summer 2026.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events.

eventCatalog.name: A chain on your block raises barista pay
eventCatalog.text: The chain two doors down posts a new starting wage.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain job postings in the area (pay must be stated in every New York City ad, so it is public).
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Chains reprice roughly once a year.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events. Independents answer with steadier schedules and tips as often as with wages.

eventCatalog.name: A chain closes stores: trained baristas on the market
eventCatalog.text: A coffee chain shuts several stores in the borough. Dozens of trained baristas are looking this month.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Announced chain closures.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The largest chain closed 54 New York City stores in September 2025 (city worker-protection agency count).
eventCatalog.note: Hiring is faster and experienced people accept the posted wage; the 3% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: More people are looking for restaurant work
eventCatalog.text: City unemployment edges up and restaurant jobs are down on the year. Your job ad gets more replies.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYS Department of Labor monthly unemployment rate and restaurant employment for New York City.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: New York City restaurant jobs were down by up to about 9,600 on the year in 2026 and unemployment stood near 4.8% in October 2026 (secondary reports of state data).
eventCatalog.note: Wages rarely fall; the 1% stands for slower raises. Figures need checking against the state series.

eventCatalog.name: Customers start skipping the tip screen
eventCatalog.text: More people tap "no tip" on the card reader. The pooled tips are down a tenth.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Quarterly average tip percentage for quick-service restaurants (Toast).
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Quick-service tips have been flat at 15.8% for seven quarters to Q2 2026; full service touched a seven-year low of 19.1% in 2025.
eventCatalog.note: A tenth off $3.13 an hour is 31 cents an hour of take-home pay; the capacity effect stands for the extra quit pressure.

eventCatalog.name: City enforcement push on protected time off
eventCatalog.text: The city worker-protection agency starts a data-driven sweep of employers with leave complaints.
eventCatalog.realSignal: City press releases on enforcement of the Protected Time Off Law.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Announced with the February 22, 2026 expansion covering 4.3 million workers.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events.

eventCatalog.name: State labor investigators target restaurants
eventCatalog.text: The state Labor Department announces record wage-theft recoveries and new investigation funding.
eventCatalog.realSignal: State Labor Department announcements and yearly recovery totals.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: More than $35 million recovered from more than 5,000 employers in 2025; wage theft has been larceny under state law since 2023.
eventCatalog.note: The 1.3 is a game-balance value.

eventCatalog.name: Federal I-9 audit notices reach restaurants
eventCatalog.text: Immigration and Customs Enforcement serves notices of inspection on food businesses.
eventCatalog.realSignal: ICE worksite enforcement announcements; revisions to its Form I-9 fact sheet.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: On March 16, 2026 ICE reclassified many common Form I-9 errors as substantive violations; fines run $288 to $2,861 per form.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events.

eventCatalog.name: Work permits end for a group of workers
eventCatalog.text: A federal protected-status program ends on a stated date.
eventCatalog.realSignal: USCIS and Federal Register notices of Temporary Protected Status terminations.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Terminations for several countries took effect in July and August 2026; about 4,800 restaurant workers were reported gone from New York City since March 2025.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events. Re-verify on the date, not before, and accept any valid document the worker chooses.

eventCatalog.name: Stomach bug goes through the team
eventCatalog.text: One sick barista becomes three.
eventCatalog.realSignal: City health department seasonal illness reports.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Winter pattern.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events. Telling sick staff to come in adds a food-safety violation to the leave violation.

eventCatalog.name: A barista is called for jury duty
eventCatalog.text: A summons arrives for one of your full-timers.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Announced to all players for the same month; county jury calls are routine.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No rate found. Juror fee $72 a day since June 8, 2025; employers with more than 10 employees pay the first three days.
eventCatalog.note: Same event as in events. A five-person shop pays nothing but must hold the job.

eventCatalog.name: A full-timer takes 12 weeks of Paid Family Leave
eventCatalog.text: One of your experienced baristas is having a child and gives you 30 days' notice of a 12-week leave.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Announced a quarter ahead to all players alike; applies to a worker with 26 weeks on the job.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No usage rate found. Benefit in 2026: 67% of pay up to $1,228.53 a week, $14,742.36 over 12 weeks, paid by the insurer.
eventCatalog.note: One of five people = 20% of hours. The wages you do not pay fund a temporary hire; the job must be held, and without the insurance the claim is yours. The 30 days' notice and the 26-week condition are from memory.

eventCatalog.name: A returning barista needs pumping breaks
eventCatalog.text: Back from leave, she needs 30 minutes two or three times a shift, and somewhere private that is not the bathroom.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A worker returns within three years of a birth.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No rate found. Since June 19, 2024 each break of up to 30 minutes is paid (Labor Law 206-c), for every employer.
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: 1 to 1.5 paid hours a shift needing cover, about 1% of team hours.

eventCatalog.name: W-2 season: staff ask where their tips are
eventCatalog.text: Your baristas want the tips on their W-2 so they can use the new federal deduction.
eventCatalog.realSignal: IRS final regulations of April 10, 2026 on the deduction for qualified tips; W-2 forms due January 31.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Applies to tax years from 2025; the deduction is capped at $25,000 and phases out above $150,000 of income.
eventCatalog.note: If cash tips were kept off payroll the staff lose the deduction and know whom to blame. The occupation code goes in box 14b of the 2026 W-2.

eventCatalog.name: Yearly harassment training is due
eventCatalog.text: A year has passed since the opening team was trained.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Twelve months since each worker's last training.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every employer, every employee, every year (Labor Law 201-g).
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic: 5 x 1 paid hour x $21.

eventCatalog.name: Snowstorm: half the team cannot get in
eventCatalog.text: Trains are suspended. Two people made it; by 11 am there are no customers and you want to close.
eventCatalog.realSignal: National Weather Service winter storm warning for New York City.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: See the weather researcher's part for storm counts.
eventCatalog.note: People who came and are sent home are owed call-in pay (3 hours). Texting before they leave home costs nothing. The 7% is two lost days.

eventCatalog.name: Heat wave behind the bar
eventCatalog.text: It is 96 degrees outside and hotter next to the espresso machine and the dish sanitizer.
eventCatalog.realSignal: National Weather Service heat advisory for New York City.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: New York has no binding indoor heat standard: the state bill with an 80-degree threshold has not passed; the mayor's June 2026 order promises guidance for indoor work by March 1, 2027.
eventCatalog.note: Extra water breaks and a second person at the bar are the moves; the 5% is my estimate. Cooling equipment is in the equipment researcher's part.

eventCatalog.name: Scenario: the City Council passes the $30 minimum wage bill
eventCatalog.text: A what-if: the first step of Int. 757 takes effect and the tipped wage starts to phase out.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Status of Int. 757 on the City Council's legislation site; as of the sources it is a proposal, not law.
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Introduced March 10, 2026: $30 by 2030 for large employers; $27 in 2030 and $29 in 2031 for small ones; no tip credit. The city's power to set a wage above the state's is disputed.
eventCatalog.note: Arithmetic for a small employer, my straight-line reading: $17 to $27 over four years is $2.50 a year, so about $19.50 in 2027; a $21 barista would expect about $1.70 more to keep the gap, +8%. The bill's own 2027 step was not in the results. Use only as a labelled scenario.
